usageRules: Every fact comes from the listed sources; cite the source when you use it.
Sales notes are interpretation, not evidence. Follow each note's 'avoid' line.
Category links mean related, not that any product would have prevented the incident.
Don't infer that a prospect or customer was affected.
Industry is the industry of the organization the source names, not a list of affected industries.

incidents.title: AI-driven intrusion campaign using a forked Cairn pentest framework
incidents.summary: Unit 42 reported that between August and September 2026 an actor it tracks as CL-STA-1238 used a customized fork of the open-source Cairn AI penetration-testing framework, running on Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek models, to conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations in the semiconductor, defense and civil-society sectors. Unit 42 confirmed unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of them; reported impacts include a persistent production API token at a semiconductor company.
uncertaintyNotes: Unit 42 assesses with moderate confidence that this is China-nexus intelligence collection; that is a hypothesis, and no actor is recorded here.
Victim organizations are unnamed; do not attribute this campaign to any specific company or customer.
This is a campaign across many organizations, typed as an intrusion because the feed's only campaign type is for malware campaigns.
Recent report (published 12 November 2026); no corrections had appeared as of 17 November 2026.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: Attackers ran an open-source AI pentest framework through 25 operations against at least 19 organizations, and got in at 10.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: If an automated agent scanned you today, what would it find first? Sprayable logins, exposed APIs, old CVEs?
salesNote.avoid: Don't name victims or state attribution as fact; Unit 42's assessment is moderate confidence.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: Victims are unnamed; the China link is a moderate-confidence assessment.

marketCategories.rationale: The operations targeted internet-facing weaknesses at the victim organizations.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That attack surface monitoring would have prevented any of the intrusions.

incidents.title: West Pharmaceutical Services intrusion with data theft and encrypted systems
incidents.summary: West Pharmaceutical Services reported in an SEC Form 8-K that an intrusion detected on 4 May 2026 involved the exfiltration of certain data by an unauthorized party and the encryption of certain systems, temporarily disrupting its business operations globally.
uncertaintyNotes: No threat actor or ransomware group is named in the filing.
Material financial impact had not been determined at filing, and the extent of the data affected was still under investigation.
The 8-K gives 7 May 2026 as its report date and was filed on 11 May 2026; the feed uses the filing date.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

sources.publisher: U.S. SEC EDGAR (West Pharmaceutical Services Form 8-K)

salesNote.headline: West Pharmaceutical's SEC filing reported data theft and encrypted systems that disrupted its operations worldwide.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: If key systems were encrypted tomorrow, which operations would stop? How fast could you restore them?
salesNote.avoid: Don't name a ransomware group or give impact figures; the filing names neither.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: The filing names no attacker and no impact figures.

marketCategories.rationale: Encrypted systems disrupted the company's operations globally, the outcome cyber recovery tools are bought to shorten.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: How West recovered, or that any product would have changed the outcome.

incidents.title: Shai-Hulud npm ecosystem compromise
incidents.summary: CISA issued an alert describing a self-replicating npm ecosystem supply-chain compromise and attempted credential theft.
uncertaintyNotes: Affected individual packages and versions require package-level primary evidence before asserting links.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: CISA flagged a self-spreading npm attack that tried to steal credentials.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: Who on your team installs npm packages? And how are your dev and CI tokens scoped and rotated?
salesNote.avoid: Do not name affected packages or suggest the account was compromised. Package-level impact is not verified here.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: Affected packages aren't verified; don't imply this account was hit.

marketCategories.rationale: CISA describes a self-replicating compromise of the npm package ecosystem, which is the risk class software supply chain tools are bought to address.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That any software supply chain product detected or would have prevented this compromise.

marketCategories.rationale: CISA reports attempted credential theft, the exposure that secrets detection and remediation tools are bought to find and respond to.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: Which credentials were taken, whether theft succeeded, or that detection would have changed the outcome.

incidents.title: s1ngularity: malicious Nx npm packages
incidents.summary: Wiz reported that malicious Nx versions published to npm on 26 August 2025 ran a post-install script that harvested GitHub and npm tokens, SSH keys and other secrets, prompting installed AI CLI tools with permission-skipping flags to search the filesystem. Wiz observed over a thousand valid GitHub tokens among the leaked data.
uncertaintyNotes: The Nx maintainers' own advisory is not yet captured as a source.
How the npm publishing token was first stolen is reported by secondary sources only.
Any relationship to the Shai-Hulud npm compromise is by ecosystem only and has not been reviewed.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: Malicious Nx packages turned developers' own AI coding tools into secret hunters. Wiz saw over a thousand valid GitHub tokens leak.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: Which AI coding tools run on your developers' machines? What can they read?
salesNote.avoid: Don't present the initial token-theft route as confirmed.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: How the publishing token was first stolen isn't confirmed.

marketCategories.rationale: Malicious versions of a widely used npm package ran a post-install script on install.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That any product in this category would have prevented it.

marketCategories.rationale: The malware harvested tokens, keys and other secrets from developer machines.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That detection would have stopped the theft, or which secrets were used afterwards.

incidents.title: tj-actions/changed-files GitHub Action compromise
incidents.summary: The GitHub advisory reports that attackers retroactively pointed multiple tj-actions/changed-files version tags at a malicious commit whose script extracted secrets from runner memory and printed them into GitHub Actions logs.
uncertaintyNotes: Reported usage of the Action (about 23,000 repositories) is not a count of confirmed leaks.
How the maintainer's token was obtained is reported elsewhere but not confirmed in this record.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: A popular GitHub Action had its version tags pointed at a malicious commit that printed CI secrets into workflow logs.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: Are your third-party Actions pinned to a commit SHA, or to tags that can move?
salesNote.avoid: The 23,000 figure is repositories using the Action, not confirmed leaks.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: About 23,000 repos used it; that's not a count of leaks.

marketCategories.rationale: A compromised third-party GitHub Action delivered malicious code into workflows that used it.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That any product in this category would have prevented it.

incidents.title: Cloud extortion campaign using exposed .env files
incidents.summary: Unit 42 reported an extortion campaign in which attackers took AWS IAM access keys from publicly exposed .env files on web applications. The campaign targeted 110,000 domains and yielded over 90,000 unique variables.
uncertaintyNotes: This is a campaign across many organizations. It is typed as an intrusion because the feed's only campaign type is for malware campaigns.
The actor and the number of extorted organizations are not stated.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: Exposed .env files handed attackers AWS keys. The campaign targeted 110,000 domains and pulled over 90,000 unique variables.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: Could one of your web apps expose its .env file? Would you notice if those keys got used?
salesNote.avoid: Don't name an actor or a number of extorted organizations; neither is stated.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: The actor and number of extorted orgs aren't stated.

marketCategories.rationale: Attackers collected cloud access keys from publicly exposed .env files.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That any product in this category would have prevented it.

marketCategories.rationale: The stolen keys were used inside victims' AWS environments, the activity cloud detection tools watch for.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That detection was absent at any victim.

incidents.title: Python admin GitHub token leaked in a Docker Hub image
incidents.summary: PyPI reported that a GitHub personal access token with admin access to the python, pypi, psf and pypa organizations was found in a compiled .pyc file inside a public Docker Hub image. The token was revoked immediately and no indicators of malicious activity were found.
uncertaintyNotes: This is a researcher-found exposure with no reported attacker activity. It is typed as a breach because the feed has no exposure type.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: An admin GitHub token for Python's core organizations was sitting in a compiled .pyc file inside a public Docker image.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: Do your secret scans cover build artifacts and container images, or just source code?
salesNote.avoid: PyPI found no malicious use; don't describe it as an attack.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: No malicious use was found; this was an exposure.

marketCategories.rationale: An admin token was exposed inside a compiled file in a public container image.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: Any malicious use; PyPI found none.

incidents.title: Cloudflare intrusion using credentials missed in rotation
incidents.summary: Cloudflare reported that it did not rotate one service token and three service accounts leaked in the October 2023 Okta compromise because it mistakenly believed they were unused. A threat actor used them between 14 and 17 November 2023 to access Cloudflare's Confluence wiki and Jira.
uncertaintyNotes: Attribution is Cloudflare's own assessment; no actor is recorded here.
The link to the Okta support-system breach has not been reviewed as a relationship.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: Four credentials Cloudflare thought were unused, left unrotated after the Okta breach, let an attacker into Confluence and Jira.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: After a vendor breach, how do you find every credential that needs rotating, even the ones you think are unused?
salesNote.avoid: Don't name an actor; attribution is Cloudflare's own assessment.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: Attribution is Cloudflare's own; don't name an actor.

marketCategories.rationale: The credentials used were a service token and service accounts that were missed in rotation.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That any product in this category would have prevented it.

incidents.title: Okta support system breach exposing session tokens in HAR files
incidents.summary: Okta reported that an actor used a service account stored in its customer support system to view files uploaded by 134 customers between 28 September and 17 October 2023. Some were HAR files containing session tokens, which the actor used to hijack the Okta sessions of 5 customers. The service account's username and password had been saved to an employee's personal Google account.
uncertaintyNotes: Okta says the credential was most likely exposed through the employee's personal Google account or personal device; the exact path is not confirmed.
Downstream incidents at Okta customers, such as Cloudflare's, are separate records; the relationship has not been reviewed.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: Okta said an attacker used a support-system service account whose password had been saved to an employee's personal Google account. They read support files from 134 customers and hijacked sessions at 5 of them.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: When your teams send HAR files or logs to a vendor's support, are session tokens stripped first? Who checks?
salesNote.avoid: Don't name a customer beyond those Okta itself named, and don't present the personal-account exposure path as confirmed.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: How the password leaked isn't confirmed.

marketCategories.rationale: Stolen session tokens were used to hijack customers' authenticated Okta sessions, the identity-layer attack ITDR tools are bought to detect.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That an ITDR tool would have detected these hijacked sessions.

marketCategories.rationale: Session tokens sat inside HAR files uploaded to a support system, and a service account password was saved to a personal account.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That scanning those files or accounts would have changed the outcome.

incidents.title: Microsoft AI research SAS token exposed 38TB
incidents.summary: Wiz Research reported that a Microsoft AI research GitHub repository shared files through an Azure SAS token scoped to the entire storage account, exposing 38TB of additional private data, including two employees' workstation backups. Wiz's timeline says Microsoft invalidated the token on 24 June 2023.
uncertaintyNotes: This is a researcher-found exposure with no reported attacker activity. It is typed as a breach because the feed has no exposure type.
Microsoft's own MSRC post is not yet captured as a source.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: One over-scoped Azure SAS token in a public GitHub repo exposed 38TB of private Microsoft research data.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: How do you keep track of the scope and expiry of shared-access tokens your teams create?
salesNote.avoid: Wiz reported no attacker activity; describe it as an exposure, not an attack.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: No attacker activity was reported; this was an exposure.

marketCategories.rationale: An over-scoped storage token was exposed through a public GitHub repository.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: Any attacker activity; none is reported.

incidents.title: Storm-0558 use of an acquired Microsoft signing key
incidents.summary: Microsoft reported that Storm-0558 used an acquired Microsoft account (MSA) consumer signing key to forge tokens and access Outlook Web Access and Outlook.com.
uncertaintyNotes: How the key left the signing environment is unknown. Microsoft's crash-dump explanation is its leading hypothesis, and its 12 March 2024 update says no crash dump containing the key material was found.
Microsoft's earlier disclosures about Storm-0558 are not captured in this record.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: Microsoft reported an attacker used an acquired consumer signing key to forge tokens and get into Outlook Web Access and Outlook.com.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: Where do your signing keys live? How would you know if key material left that environment?
salesNote.avoid: Don't state how the key was stolen; Microsoft has not confirmed it.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: How the key left Microsoft is still unconfirmed.

incidents.title: CircleCI breach via malware on an engineer's laptop
incidents.summary: CircleCI reported that malware on an engineer's laptop was used to steal a valid, 2FA-backed SSO session, and recommended that all customers rotate secrets stored in the platform. CircleCI first alerted customers on 4 January 2023 and published its incident report on 12 January.
uncertaintyNotes: Impact on individual customers is not covered by this record.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: Malware on one engineer's laptop stole a 2FA-backed SSO session. CircleCI told every customer to rotate their stored secrets.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: If your CI vendor asked you to rotate every stored secret today, how long would it take?
salesNote.avoid: Don't claim specific customer impact; the source covers the rotation advice, not individual customers.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: Impact on individual customers isn't covered.

marketCategories.rationale: CircleCI told all customers to rotate secrets stored in its platform, the rotation work secrets management tools are bought for.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That any tool would have avoided the rotation.

incidents.title: Toyota T-Connect access key exposed on public GitHub
incidents.summary: Toyota reported that a T-Connect website development contractor uploaded part of the site's source code, including a data server access key, to a public GitHub repository in December 2017. The code stayed public until 15 September 2022 and the key was changed on 17 September 2022. Up to 296,019 customer email addresses and customer management numbers may have been exposed.
uncertaintyNotes: Toyota says third-party access could not be confirmed from access history but could not be ruled out; no misuse had been confirmed. It is typed as a breach because the feed has no exposure type.
Toyota's notice is in Japanese; this summary is a translated paraphrase.
Hard-coded credentials (CWE-798) is a weakness candidate only.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: Toyota said a contractor left a data server access key in public GitHub code for almost five years, putting up to 296,019 customer records at risk.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: Do your contractors' repos fall under your secret scanning, or only your own?
salesNote.avoid: Toyota could not confirm the key was used; don't describe it as a confirmed theft.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: Toyota couldn't confirm the key was ever used.

marketCategories.rationale: A data server access key sat in a public GitHub repository for nearly five years.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That the key was used; Toyota could not confirm it.

incidents.title: Uber intrusion via a compromised contractor account and MFA push approval
incidents.summary: Uber reported that an attacker compromised an external contractor's account, likely using a corporate password bought on the dark web after malware infected the contractor's personal device. The attacker repeatedly triggered two-factor login approval requests until the contractor accepted one, then reached other employee accounts with elevated permissions to tools including G-Suite and Slack, and downloaded some internal Slack messages and invoice-tool information. Uber says it did not see access to production systems, user accounts or sensitive user databases.
uncertaintyNotes: Uber attributes the attack to Lapsus$; as with other vendor attributions in this feed, no actor is recorded.

Reports that the attacker found a PowerShell script with hard-coded admin credentials for Uber's PAM system come from the attacker's own statements and secondary coverage. Uber's statement does not mention it, so it is not part of this record.
Distinct from incident:uber-github-aws-key-2016 (different year and method).
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: An attacker used a contractor's bought password and kept sending MFA push requests until one got approved. From there they moved into Slack and G-Suite.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: Do your contractors use push-approval MFA? Would you notice a burst of denied prompts?
salesNote.avoid: Don't repeat the hard-coded PAM credential story; Uber's statement doesn't support it.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: Uber says it saw no access to production systems or user databases.

marketCategories.rationale: A contractor's corporate account was taken over through a bought password and an accepted MFA push request.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That a different MFA method would certainly have stopped it.

marketCategories.rationale: After the first account, the attacker reached other employee accounts with elevated permissions.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That an ITDR tool would have detected this activity.

incidents.title: Codecov Bash Uploader compromise
incidents.summary: Codecov reported that a credential exposed by an error in its Docker image creation process let an actor modify its Bash Uploader script, which could then export information from customers' CI environments. Codecov says it learned of the change on 1 April 2021.
uncertaintyNotes: Which customers' secrets were actually used is not established.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: One leaked credential let an attacker change Codecov's Bash Uploader and pull data out of customers' CI environments.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: What third-party scripts run in your CI today, and which secrets can they see?
salesNote.avoid: Don't say which customers lost secrets; that is not established.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: Which customers actually lost secrets is unknown.

marketCategories.rationale: A modified third-party script ran inside customers' CI pipelines, the supplier risk software supply chain tools address.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That any product in this category would have prevented it.

incidents.title: SolarWinds Orion supply-chain compromise
incidents.summary: CISA reported active exploitation involving affected SolarWinds Orion software versions.
uncertaintyNotes: Exact occurrence date, complete victim list and attack-technique links are outside this seed's verified scope.

salesNote.headline: CISA reported attackers actively exploiting affected versions of SolarWinds Orion.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: How does your team decide which vendor updates to trust? Who owns that check?
salesNote.avoid: Do not claim any product would have prevented it. The victim list and attack techniques are outside this record's verified scope.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: Older incident (2020); victims and methods aren't covered here.

marketCategories.rationale: CISA reported active exploitation involving affected versions of a vendor's software, the risk of trusting third-party software that software supply chain tools address.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: How the affected versions were altered, which is outside this record's verified scope, or that any product would have prevented it.

marketCategories.rationale: The exploited software came from a third-party vendor, which is the exposure third-party risk programs assess.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That a vendor risk assessment would have revealed this compromise.

incidents.title: Uber S3 breach via an AWS key in a private GitHub repository
incidents.summary: The FTC states that between 13 October and 15 November 2016 intruders accessed Uber's Amazon S3 datastore using an AWS access key posted in a private GitHub repository. The intruders reached the repository with passwords exposed in other breaches, and Uber did not require multi-factor authentication for GitHub. Uber disclosed the breach on 21 November 2017.
uncertaintyNotes: Hard-coded credentials (CWE-798) is a weakness candidate only.
The captured FTC document does not show its own publication date.
No ATT&CK technique is asserted until a separate sourced mapping review.

salesNote.headline: Per the FTC, intruders used reused passwords to get into a private GitHub repo, found an AWS key and reached Uber's S3 data.
salesNote.discoveryQuestion: Do you scan private repos for cloud keys? Is MFA required on your code host?
salesNote.avoid: This happened in 2016; don't present it as recent.
salesNote.sellerCaveat: This was 2016; use it as a lesson, not news.

marketCategories.rationale: An AWS access key stored in a private GitHub repository gave the intruders access to S3.
marketCategories.doesNotImply: That scanning was absent, or that it would have changed the outcome.
